items.prompt: What is the outer skeleton of an insect called?

options.label: An internal skeleton
options.feedback: Insects do not have an internal skeleton; their support comes from the outside.

options.label: An exoskeleton
options.feedback: Correct. The hard outer layer that protects and supports the insect is the exoskeleton.

options.label: A soft body wall
options.feedback: Insects have a hard outer layer, not a soft one, although the hardness varies between species.

options.label: A shell made of bone
options.feedback: The exoskeleton is made of chitin, not bone, and it is external.

items.ok_line: The exoskeleton is the insect's hard outer covering.
items.ko_line: Remember, the skeleton is outside the body.
items.exp_text: The exoskeleton is a hard outer layer, made mostly of chitin, that protects and supports the insect's body. Unlike a backbone, it is on the outside.

items.prompt: Into how many main sections is an insect's body divided?

options.label: Three
options.feedback: Yes, the head, thorax, and abdomen are the three main body sections.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Insects have three body regions, not two; the head and thorax are separate.

options.label: Four
options.feedback: There are only three main parts; the legs and wings are attached to the thorax but are not body sections.

options.label: One solid piece
options.feedback: The body is divided into three distinct regions, even though they are connected.

items.ok_line: Insects have three main body parts.
items.ko_line: Count the head, thorax, and abdomen.
items.exp_text: Every insect has a head, a thorax, and an abdomen. These three regions are called tagmata and each does a different job.

items.prompt: What material is an insect's exoskeleton mostly made of?

options.label: Calcium carbonate
options.feedback: Calcium carbonate can harden chitin, but it is not the main material; chitin is the base.

options.label: Keratin
options.feedback: Keratin is found in hair and nails, not in insect exoskeletons.

options.label: Chitin
options.feedback: Correct. Chitin is the long-chain polymer that forms the bulk of the exoskeleton.

options.label: Cellulose
options.feedback: Cellulose is a plant material, not a component of insect exoskeletons.

items.ok_line: Chitin makes up most of the hard outer layer.
items.ko_line: Look for the polymer called chitin.
items.exp_text: The exoskeleton is built from chitin, a strong, flexible material. Chitin can be modified to become harder, but it is always the main ingredient.

items.prompt: Which part of an insect's body is mainly specialized for locomotion?

options.label: The head
options.feedback: The head is for sensing and feeding, not for moving around.

options.label: The thorax
options.feedback: Yes, the thorax anchors the legs and wings, so it handles locomotion.

options.label: The abdomen
options.feedback: The abdomen handles digestion, respiration, excretion, and reproduction—not movement.

options.label: The exoskeleton
options.feedback: The exoskeleton is the covering, not a body section; the thorax is the moving part.

items.ok_line: The thorax powers walking and flying.
items.ko_line: Legs and wings attach to the thorax.
items.exp_text: The thorax is the middle section. It carries the legs and wings, so it is the part specialized for movement.

items.prompt: How many pairs of legs does an insect have?

options.label: One pair
options.feedback: One pair would be just two legs, but insects have six legs.

options.label: Two pairs
options.feedback: That is four legs, but insects have six.

options.label: Five pairs
options.feedback: That would be ten legs, too many for an insect.

options.label: Three pairs
options.feedback: Correct. Three pairs means a total of six legs, all attached to the thorax.

items.ok_line: Insects always have three pairs of legs.
items.ko_line: Count the pairs: three make six legs.
items.exp_text: All insects have three pairs of legs. These six legs attach to the three segments of the thorax.

items.prompt: Where are an insect's mouthparts located?

options.label: Outside the head capsule
options.feedback: Yes, the mouthparts stick out from the head capsule, which is a key insect feature.

options.label: Inside the head capsule
options.feedback: The mouthparts are not inside the head; they project outward from it.

options.label: On the thorax
options.feedback: The thorax carries legs and wings, not mouthparts.

options.label: At the tip of the abdomen
options.feedback: The abdomen is for digestion and reproduction, not for mouthparts.

items.ko_line: They are external to the head capsule.
items.exp_text: Insects have mouthparts located outside the head capsule. This external position separates them from their closest relatives, the non-insect hexapods.

items.prompt: Which body section of an insect is specialized for digestion, respiration, excretion, and reproduction?

options.label: The head
options.feedback: The head is for sensing and eating, not for digestion or reproduction.

options.label: The thorax
options.feedback: The thorax is for movement, not for these internal functions.

options.label: The abdomen
options.feedback: Correct. The abdomen handles digestion, respiration, excretion, and reproduction.

options.label: The exoskeleton
options.feedback: The exoskeleton is the outer shell and does not do those jobs.

items.ok_line: The abdomen handles life's internal tasks.
items.exp_text: The abdomen is the rear section. It is where digestion, respiration, excretion, and reproduction take place.

items.prompt: What are the two layers of the insect cuticle called?

options.label: The tergum and the sternum
options.feedback: Those are parts of a body segment, not layers of the cuticle.

options.label: The epicuticle and the procuticle
options.feedback: Correct. The thin outer epicuticle and the thicker inner procuticle are the two layers.

options.label: The exocuticle and the endocuticle
options.feedback: Those are sublayers inside the procuticle, not the two main layers.

options.label: The notum and the pleuron
options.feedback: Those are regions of a segment, not cuticle layers.

items.ko_line: Look at the two major layers, not their subparts.
items.exp_text: The cuticle has an outer thin, waxy epicuticle and a much thicker inner procuticle. The procuticle itself contains the exocuticle and endocuticle.

items.prompt: How many segments make up the insect thorax?

options.label: Three
options.feedback: Correct. The prothorax, mesothorax, and metathorax are the three thoracic segments.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: There are three, not two; the mesothorax and metathorax are separate.

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Only three segments form the thorax.

options.label: Six
options.feedback: Six is the total number of legs, not the number of thoracic segments.

items.ko_line: Pro-, meso-, and metathorax make three.
items.exp_text: The thorax is made of three segments: the prothorax near the head, the mesothorax in the middle, and the metathorax next to the abdomen.

items.prompt: What process allows an insect's exoskeleton to grow along with the insect?

options.label: Shedding the entire body
options.feedback: The insect sheds only its old cuticle, not its whole body.

options.label: Stretching the cuticle
options.feedback: The cuticle cannot stretch to grow; it must be replaced.

options.label: Building new layers on top
options.feedback: New layers form after the old cuticle is shed, not on top of it.

options.label: Molting
options.feedback: Yes, molting is the periodic shedding of the old cuticle so a new, larger one can form.

items.ok_line: Molting lets the exoskeleton be replaced.
items.ko_line: The cuticle cannot grow, so it is shed.
items.exp_text: Because the exoskeleton cannot grow, the insect sheds it in a process called molting. The old cuticle separates and is replaced by a new, larger one.
